title: The bramble king (Judges 9:7–15)
hook: Jotham's fable: olive, fig and vine refuse to rule; only the bramble wants to

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three hundred with jars and torches. Your line was fewer is enough. Today, Gideon is gone, and one of his sons wants to be king.

A voice shouts down from the top of Mount Gerizim to the city of Shechem below. It's Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon, alive because he hid. His half-brother Abimelech has just murdered the rest of the brothers, and the men of Shechem have made Abimelech king. Jotham can't fight him. So he tells them a story about trees. Hearken unto me, he calls down, that God may hearken unto you.
screen: `A VOICE FROM MOUNT GERIZIM.` → `ONE BROTHER ESCAPED.` → `A STORY ABOUT TREES.`

segments.voice: Once, the trees went out to anoint a king. They asked the olive: reign over us. Should I give up my oil, it said, that honors God and people, to go and sway over the trees? They asked the fig. Should I give up my sweetness and my good fruit? They asked the vine. Should I give up my wine, that cheers God and people? Each has real work to do, and won't trade it for a crown. Last, they go to the bramble, a low thorny bush with no fruit worth picking. And the bramble says yes. Come and take shelter in my shade. Some readers smile at that: a bramble has almost no shade to give. Then, in the same breath, a threat: "and if not, let fire come out of the bramble, and devour the cedars of Lebanon." So the fable says two things. The ones with something to give were too busy giving it. The one with nothing to give wanted the crown most, and promised shelter while warning of fire. Jotham turns it on Shechem: if you've dealt honestly with my father's house, enjoy your king. If not, let fire come out of Abimelech and burn you, and fire come out of you and burn him. Then he runs. In the end, Shechem and Abimelech turn on each other and both are destroyed, and the text says the curse of Jotham came upon them.
screen: `OLIVE, FIG AND VINE SAY NO.` · `THE BRAMBLE SAYS YES.` · `SHADE OFFERED, FIRE THREATENED.` · `THE CURSE COMES TRUE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one group you belong to, a family, a team, a group chat, and notice, without judging anyone, who quietly bears fruit there and who wants the crown. Then turn it gently on yourself: where are you the olive tree, and where are you the bramble?
bramble. The low thorny bush in Jotham's fable, the only tree with nothing to give that still said yes to the crown.
Your line: the bramble wants the crown. The olive was too busy giving oil. That's day seven hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Jews study Jotham's fable in Judges 9 as part of the Former Prophets; it is often read alongside Gideon's refusal of kingship in Judges 8 when teachers discuss power and leadership.

fork.setup: you're the olive tree. all the trees come to you and say: reign over us. what do you say?
options: should I give up my oil, that honors God and people, to sway over the trees?
only if the fig agrees too.
fork.reveal: the olive says no, and so do the fig and the vine. only the bramble says yes, and it threatens fire if it isn't obeyed.

original.note: Hebrew: a thornbush, the bramble that wants to be king in Jotham's fable.

what it means: the ones with fruit to give won't trade it for a crown, and the one with nothing to give wants it most.
what a scholar hears: by the end of the chapter, the text says the curse of Jotham came upon them (Judges 9:20, 9:56–57).

chat.says: In Jotham's fable, why does the bramble end up king instead of the olive or the fig?
options: The fruitful trees wouldn't give up their gifts, and the one with nothing to give wanted it most.
The bramble was the strongest tree, so the others gladly chose it to protect them.
The olive and fig were too lazy to rule, so the fable praises the hard-working bramble.
chat.meaning: The olive, fig and vine won't trade their fruit for a crown; the bramble, with nothing to give, says yes and threatens fire.

Jotham.meaning: Gideon's youngest son, who escaped and told the fable

Abimelech.meaning: Gideon's son who killed his brothers and was made king

Gerizim.meaning: the mountain above Shechem where Jotham shouted his fable

Shechem.meaning: the city whose men made Abimelech king

sources.quoted: and if not, let fire come out of the bramble, and devour the cedars of Lebanon.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): deep-read against Judges and the cited rabbinic sources; no changes needed.
Judges 9:15 quoted from the KJV; the JPS 1917 wording is believed identical for this phrase but was not verified.
'In the end' replaces the text's three years (9:22) to keep numbers out.
Abimelech's brothers are 'the rest of the brothers' rather than the text's count (9:5), to keep numbers out of the hook.
'A bramble has almost no shade to give' is offered as 'some readers smile at that', a common reading, not a claim of the text.
Atad as 'thornbush/bramble' follows the plain lexicon gloss; exact botanical identification is disputed and left out.
Editor: the teach's last line no longer says fire came true 'on both sides' (Abimelech dies by a millstone, not fire, 9:53); it now cites 9:57, the curse of Jotham came upon them.
